summary:
Djibouti's penal code contains no express offence criminalising consensual same-sex conduct. Sections 353 and 354 refer vaguely to "good morals" and public morality without naming same-sex relations, and no provision states the position either way. Outright International's country overview, updated 12 March 2026, nevertheless marks same-sex relations as not lawful throughout the country in its at-a-glance assessment, and authorities retain the power to prosecute public same-sex conduct under these articles. The practical position is that such conduct is treated as de facto illegal despite the absence of an express offence.

The same overview records that Djibouti has no legal gender recognition: there is no procedure by which a person's sex marker can be amended on official documents. A trans visitor's foreign documents are therefore assessed against a framework that offers no domestic equivalent of recognition.

Protection against discrimination is narrow. The US State Department's 2023 Human Rights Report states that Djibouti law contains no prohibition of discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the employment field is the only area in which any protection is recorded. There is no general legal remedy for a person refused service, housing or entry to a facility on those grounds.

Complaints of mistreatment can be filed with the police or with the national human-rights commission (CNDH), which is the documented route of recourse. The 2023 report cites no cases of official violence against LGBTI people, and it describes a societal pattern of discrimination rather than documented state action. No reported case law defines the outer limits of Sections 353 and 354, so the exposure of a trans visitor who is visible, or who engages in any conduct in a public setting that would be read as same-sex, cannot be bounded from the sources.

The 2023 report describes status and conduct as taboo, with pervasive social and religious intolerance recorded in that year, and notes that people fear family and community shunning on disclosure. Documentation of the position is thin: a Canadian Refugee Protection Division research request covering 2009 to March 2012 found that information on the treatment of sexual minorities was scarce across all consulted sources, and no later incident-level documentation appears in this inventory.
tangentialFactors:
The US State Department's 2015 Human Rights Report on Djibouti contains limited LGBT-specific content; its substantive material covers general country conditions, including suppression of the opposition, harsh prison conditions, female genital mutilation and trafficking. Those conditions bear on the risk of detention for any traveller but are not specific to gender identity.

The documentation baseline for this jurisdiction is unusually sparse. The Canadian research request of 2009 to March 2012 relied largely on a single US country report, indicating how little legal, protection or support-service framework was recorded in that period. Later sources in this inventory are country-wide human-rights assessments rather than trans-specific studies, so the absence of recorded incidents should be read as an absence of documentation, not as evidence of a settled position.
localsOnly:
LGBTI organisations cannot register in Djibouti, so there is no legally constituted domestic advocacy or support body operating under that description. Outright International's overview of 12 March 2026 records this alongside the absence of legal gender recognition.

Discrimination protection extends to employment only, and no law prohibits discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity more broadly, per the US State Department's 2023 report. Residents have a documented channel for complaints through the police and the national human-rights commission (CNDH).

Social conditions recorded in 2023 include status and conduct treated as taboo, pervasive social and religious intolerance, and fear of family and community shunning on disclosure. Public societal discussion of homosexuality is not tolerated, and the "good morals" provisions of Sections 353 and 354 remain the instruments under which public conduct can be prosecuted.
outOfScopeNotes:
No reported case law defines the scope of Sections 353 and 354, so how far the "good morals" and public-morality provisions reach in practice is unresolved on these sources. Whether a foreign passport bearing an amended gender marker affects entry, visa issuance or airport processing in Djibouti is not sourced here and remains unresolved.

No dated incident of violence against a trans person, and no trans-specific prevalence figure with a denominator, appears in this inventory; the 2023 report cites no official violence cases. The most recent source in the inventory is the Outright International overview updated 12 March 2026, which supplies the legal-status assessment but no incident data. The 2015 US country report and the Canadian research request covering 2009 to March 2012 are historical baselines only and should not be read as describing the present position.
